Hi, it’s Firas!

I’m a journalist. My work has led me to collaborate and appear, among other things, with internationally broadcast media on issues relating to the Maghreb and, more broadly, the Arab world.
Depuis le 7 octobre 2023, le monde arabe: Since October 7, 2023, the Arab world has been living to the rhythm of a new and particularly violent war in the Middle East. As we take stock of a year of horrors, a new country has been deeply wounded: Lebanon.
Face au déluge de violence qui submerge:
Faced with the deluge of violence engulfing the region, some live in exile to the rhythm of their loved ones’ suffering. My intention is to make their voices heard amid the clamour of news dispatches and to bring a bit of humanity to this context for the length of a read!

It would have been entirely possible, in this article, to describe at greater length the current stakes of this multi-party conflict. Or to delve deeper into Lebanon’s internal dynamics. But that would overlook what is most urgent: the difficult existence that Lebanese people, both in the country and in the diaspora, are living today.

The great challenge of this article lay in accurately conveying the feelings of the people I interviewed in Lebanon. They are going through a very difficult time. Despite my knowledge of the region and its context, it is hard for me to truly grasp what a person feels when faced with yet another crisis and yet another trauma.
À travers cet article, j’ai pu échanger:
Throughout this article, I was able to work with the team, who helped me convey as sincerely as possible the feelings described and the words I gathered. They also helped me characterize current events and their context with precision, so that I could present an article that is accessible and relevant to anyone shaken by the ongoing tragedies.

Fin septembre 2024. La crainte d’une opé: Late September 2024. The fear of a violent military operation, one that could only have a heavy toll, hangs over a country already worn out by decades of political and economic crises.
À 9 000 km de là, Carine Ghali et Farah: 9,000 km away, Carine Ghali and Farah El-Bizri, two Lebanese women, met us at one of their Montréal haunts. Together, we talk about their daily lives in exile amid this explosive situation in the Middle East.
« Le Liban est instable depuis longtemps: “Lebanon has been unstable for a long time, too long...” says Farah, settling back into the large, comfortable couch at the plush Tommy Café on Sainte-Catherine Street in Montréal. “From October 7 [2023], I felt that Lebanon would be hit at some point.” Nervous, she picks up her phone to answer a text.
Originaire de Saïda, Farah est arrivée a: Originally from Sidon, Farah arrived in Canada in the summer of 2006, at the age of 15. She landed in Montréal after a perilous journey to Syria, fleeing the war then underway between Israel and Hezbollah. From Montréal, she keeps a close watch on the successive crises her country is going through.
Nous l’avons rencontrée à l’issue d’une: We met her after a demonstration on Saturday, September 28, 2024. <l1>More than 700 people had gathered </l1>in Montréal to express their anger at the deluge of bombs dropped on southern Lebanon and the southern suburbs of Beirut.
Lors de notre entretien, Farah semble ma: During our interview, Farah seems shaken by the turn of events. “The building where I lived in Beirut five years ago was destroyed last week. I can’t believe it. It’s a nightmare. Going home will now only be a memory,” she confides. Her flat voice betrays a habituation to these tragedies. Indeed, Lebanon’s Ministry of Health <l1>recently announced</l1> a tragic toll of 2,350 dead in Lebanon since October 7, 2023.
Deux jours plus tard, nous retrouvons Ca: Two days later, we meet Carine in the early evening at a café near Atwater. Only three days have passed since the assassination of Hassan Nasrallah, the leader of Hezbollah. An eerily calm atmosphere reigns in the place, with employees and customers glued to their phones. Connected to the same ills, those of their country.
Carine a quitté le Liban à 29 ans, en 20: Carine left Lebanon at 29, in 2022, two years after the devastating explosion at the Port of Beirut. “It was an apocalypse in just three minutes... The country’s economic situation couldn’t withstand such a catastrophe. The future in Lebanon became impossible for me,” she says, sadness in her eyes.
En effet, le pays du Cèdre subit depuis: Indeed, for a decade the Land of the Cedar has suffered from political paralysis, exacerbated by a locked-in multi-confessional system set up at the end of the civil war. This situation has stalled all economic and social progress.
Le statu quo institutionnel, combiné à u: The institutional status quo, combined with endemic corruption, has driven the country into an economic crisis that the World Bank considers one of the <l1>most severe since the mid-19</l1><sup><l1>th</l1></sup><l1> century.</l1>
En 2020, l’explosion du port de Beyrouth: In 2020, the explosion at the Port of Beirut dealt a fatal blow to the country, causing numerous shortages. Since that tragedy, the inflation rate has reached alarming levels.
« Mes journées, c’est X [anciennement Tw: “My days are X [formerly Twitter, editor’s note] and Insta, then refresh, refresh, refresh...” Carine describes, energetically miming the motion. By the time we meet her, the Israeli army is preparing a ground incursion into southern Lebanon. Later that night, Iran would fire nearly 200 missiles at Israel, claiming a single victim. A Palestinian man, fatally struck by debris in Jericho in the West Bank.
Carine devait visiter ses parents au pay: Carine was supposed to visit her parents in Lebanon two weeks before our meeting, but nothing went as planned. She speaks of this disappointment pragmatically: “If the flight was cancelled, maybe it’s a sign from fate. It’s safer. But I’m always ready to go!” she says. Her words reflect her torn state between the obligation to stay and the desire to leave…

Nous questionnons Carine au sujet de l’<: We ask Carine about the pager explosions of September 17. “It was [like] something out of Black Mirror. Innocent people also died or were injured, but no condemnation!” she exclaims. Indeed, neither Canada nor the United States condemned these explosions, which maimed and killed many civilians. Israel’s military methods, often <l1>described as destructive and disproportionate</l1> by international NGOs, made her fear the worst. “Only Israel can level [a residential complex] to kill a single person with complete impunity,” adds Carine, a former Beirut resident, referring to the operation that led to the death of Hassan Nasrallah, the former secretary general of Hezbollah.
« En voyant des images de la banlieue su: “Seeing images of Beirut’s southern suburbs on September 23, I had a flashback of the 2020 explosion. I felt like the attack was happening in my bedroom. I almost fainted,” says Carine. “I couldn’t stay alone, I was at rock bottom,” she adds, glancing at the entrance of BHive Café. Her distress gives way, fleetingly, to a smile, then a wave of the hand.
C’est son frère jumeau qui nous salue. L: It’s her twin brother greeting us. He also left Lebanon for Montréal in 2022. Coffee in hand, the civil engineer seems a regular here and joins friends to talk about the latest news from Lebanon.
« Le café BHive est devenu notre repère: “BHive Café has become our spot for the past 10 days. There are several of us Lebanese here. We can talk and understand each other. It’s our situation room,” says Carine. She too has become a regular over the last few days.
Aux craintes que suscite le bilan humain: On top of the fears raised by the human and economic toll of this conflict comes a new worry: that of being abandoned by the world and its complex power relations.
Farah, de passage ce mardi au café pour: Farah, stopping by the café this Tuesday for her new ritual, catches up on the news at the next table, then joins us.
Les deux trentenaires éprouvent dans leu: In their daily lives, the two women, both in their thirties, feel a lack of compassion for what Lebanese people are going through. “[What’s happening in Lebanon] is a subject everyone avoids [colleagues, acquaintances]. Even when they ask for news, it’s furtive. Right after, they go back to talking about the nice weather,” explains Farah. Vehement, she continues: “Our dead never have a story. I sometimes wonder whether the world is indifferent to us or hates us. But we’ve gotten used to it!”
Farah et Carine le savent, après le calm: Farah and Carine know it: after the calm comes the storm. They are about to experience solitude in the eye of the cyclone. “Exile is hard to live with; daily life becomes meaningless. Nothing matters when your country is being bombed,” says Farah, palms open as if stating the obvious.
« C’est glaçant de recevoir des messages: “It’s chilling to get messages that start with ‘If you can’t find me later.’ Even if it’s in a light tone, it foreshadows the worst,” she adds, less assured.
« Être avec la communauté libanaise en c: “Being with the Lebanese community during this difficult time has its advantages, but also its drawbacks. It’s comforting to share our fears, but some tragedies are intimate,” continues Farah, gravely. The lack of sleep already shows on her face.
Carine appelle ses parents et ses grands: Carine calls her parents and grandparents every day, but the anguish is palpable on the other end of the line: “My grandfather has lost his appetite. I talk to him often. Sometimes I joke around with the names of fruits to get him smiling again. But I don’t always manage,” she laments. “My parents are in a safe place in Beirut. But ‘safe’ in Beirut is only five minutes by car from where the attacks and bombings are happening,” she explains, swallowing the last drops of her evening cortado.
Les bombardements israéliens ont poussé: Israeli bombings have pushed many people onto the roads. As of October 7, 2024, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees counts <l1>1.2 million displaced people</l1>, more than 15% of Lebanon’s population. On the ground, the situation is difficult for these families seeking refuge in the north of the country.
Carine décrit un grand écart émotionnel: Carine describes an emotional tightrope far from her loved ones: “My life is on pause, my people are suffering, it’s a nightmare. I sometimes feel guilty for being safe here in Montréal, terrified by the images of my country under the bombs. I don’t know how long this will last,” she continues, pale.
« Mes amis m’ont parlé de familles bloqu: “My friends told me about families stuck for 17 hours on the road with children, without food, for a trip that should normally take only 45 minutes,” describes Carine, her voice trembling.
Pendant que les déplacés s’entassent sur:
While displaced people pile up on the roads, Farah’s mother, a seasoned humanitarian worker, is getting ready to board the first plane leaving Montréal for Lebanon. She has chosen to go despite the advice of her contacts on the ground, who discourage her from making the trip.

She runs <l1>Bluemission</l1>, an NGO founded in 2022 to help rural and refugee women in Sidon, the country’s third-largest city, access health care, including mental health care, and education. For her, Farah explains, it is a call of duty in these times of distress for all Lebanese women.
Sa fille se sent démunie. « Elle sera ut: Her daughter feels helpless. “She’ll be useful there, unlike me here. Her absence will be another ordeal for me and my whole family,” she adds. Although she understands her mother’s motivations, Farah’s indecision and worry linger under her cloud of smoke, outside the café.

Carine, une coach sportive, a réuni sur: Carine, a fitness coach, gathered enthusiasts along the Lachine Canal<l1> for a workout session</l1> in support of the <l2>Lebanese Red Cross</l2>. “It’s the best way to help from Montréal. Every dollar counts!” she says.
« J’ai été surprise de voir autant de ge: “I was surprised to see so many people of different nationalities come to work out and make significant donations. It was incredible. I feel truly useful!” she concludes proudly. Her initiative raised $1,470 in donations.

“The Lebanese diaspora is huge. I hope the international community will step in to save my country. But it’s hard not to think [also] about Gaza,” says Farah, speaking of the future in the Middle East.

Indeed, by conservative estimates, the Israeli army has killed at least <l1>42,000 Gazans</l1> in a year of massive bombardment. “Their weapons are much more powerful than in 2006!” exclaims Carine, implying that the IDF’s will to destroy is more pronounced today than it was 18 years ago.
Jusqu’à présent, l’armée israélienne n’a: So far, the Israeli army has not specified its intentions regarding the ground operation in Lebanon, despite the presence of UN peacekeeping forces in the south of the country since 2000. The risk of getting bogged down in a lasting conflict is being considered.
Un tel enlisement est redouté par la dia: The diaspora dreads such a quagmire. “We Lebanese must be united and move past our political and religious divisions. It’s our salvation,” Farah insists. Carine dreams of a future in which the country can rebuild. “I believe in our resilience. We’ve been through so many trials and we’re still here.”
Une deuxième année de tension se profile: A second year of tension looms in the Middle East, and in Lebanon in particular. Calls for a ceasefire, issued through every channel, seem to have no effect. Meanwhile, international efforts to avoid a regional war, or an even wider one, are multiplying. Bullets and bombs resound, striking the hearts and minds of those living in exile, like Carine and Farah, who are also victims of this conflict.
